title: Ada and the Parish
premise: Estate lawyer Petra Villalobos is hired to read the will of Edmund Parish, a recluse whose death certificate was signed a full week before his funeral — yet the will is dated three days after that. Buried in its clauses is a confession naming a witness, Ada, whom every record insists died twenty years ago. As Petra traces the impossible dates, she realizes Edmund faked his own death to protect Ada from someone still living in the village, and that the postmarked confession was meant for Petra specifically because she once survived something similar. The witness everyone swears is dead turns out to be Edmund's daughter, hiding in plain sight as the parish archivist, and Petra must choose between exposing the truth — which will destroy Ada's fragile safety — and burying a murder that Edmund committed to keep her alive. In the end, Petra burns the confession, files a doctored will, and walks away carrying the same secret she once needed someone else to carry for her.
about_author: Wren Eastwick spent a decade working in probate offices in the north of England, where the strangest stories arrived not in manuscripts but in filing cabinets. 'Ada and the Parish' is their first novel, drawn from the paperwork no one ever asks to read.

chapters.title: The Reading of a Dead Man's Will
chapters.summary: Petra Villalobos, third-person POV, arrives at the rain-soaked village of Marlow St. Cuthbert to read the will of Edmund Parish. The reading proceeds normally until she notices the will's date falls after the death certificate's date. Emotional beat: quiet professional unease hardening into suspicion.

chapters.title: Postmarked the Day After
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. A letter arrives at her office, postmarked the day after Edmund's funeral, containing a half-finished confession and the single name: Ada. The handwriting matches the will. Beat: dread — the dead man is writing to her from beyond a lie.

chapters.title: The Archivist in the Tower
chapters.summary: Third-person POV shifting between Petra and Ada, the parish archivist who catalogs records no one reads. Ada recognizes Petra's name on the visitor log and quietly removes a file. Beat: two hunters circling the same archive, each pretending not to see the other.

chapters.title: A Death Certificate Signed in Advance
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. She pulls Edmund's medical records and finds the doctor who signed the certificate retired the same week — and has since vanished. Beat: the machinery of Edmund's fake death was professional, expensive, and terrified.

chapters.title: What the Village Remembers
chapters.summary: Petra interviews villagers under the guise of settling the estate. Everyone loved Edmund; everyone remembers a daughter who died at sea twenty years ago. Beat: grief so uniform it feels rehearsed.

chapters.title: The Room Behind the Vestry
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She retrieves a locked case from behind the vestry wall — photographs, a passport in her dead name, and a letter from her father: 'If anyone comes asking, you were never born.' Beat: loyalty as a cage built with love.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Ada's POV. The night her mother drowned and Edmund confessed to Petra's predecessor, a young lawyer who helped bury the truth. Beat: the origin of the secret, and Petra's unknowing inheritance of it.

chapters.title: Someone Is Reading the Mail
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Her office is searched; the confession letter is photographed, not stolen. Whoever it is wants her to know she's being watched. Beat: the mystery turns from puzzle to threat.

chapters.title: The Retired Doctor's Cottage
chapters.summary: Petra finds the vanished doctor living under a new name two counties away. He tells her Edmund paid him to kill a man on paper — and that someone else asked him last week the same questions. Beat: a race she is already losing.

chapters.title: Ada, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A stranger attends Sunday service, asking the vicar about parish records. Ada recognizes the questions as the ones she dreads. Beat: survival means performing grief for your own funeral all over again.

chapters.title: Two Women, One Confession
chapters.summary: Petra and Ada meet openly at last, each pretending to be something she isn't. Ada lies beautifully; Petra lets her. Beat: a duel of omissions where both leave certain they were the one being deceived.

chapters.title: The Clause No One Questioned
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Rereading the will, she finds Edmund left everything to 'my daughter, should she live' — a legal impossibility that forces her to prove Ada is alive to execute it, or destroy the will to keep her hidden. Beat: the trap of the law itself.

chapters.title: What Edmund Did
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, full revelation. Her mother discovered Edmund's brother was selling information that would have exposed Ada's true parentage and endangered her; Edmund's confession is not to a murder he committed but one he failed to prevent — and then covered up. Beat: the moral floor drops out.

chapters.title: The Man from the Probate Office
chapters.summary: Third-person. The watcher reveals himself: an investigator hired by Edmund's brother's son, who suspects the will defrauds him and wants Ada declared dead — permanently. Beat: the price of survival becomes literal.

chapters.title: Petra's Own Buried Year
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. She confronts why she took this case: twenty years ago someone falsified a record to save her, and she has spent her career inside paperwork, invisible. Beat: the theme of loyalty vs. truth turns inward.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The investigator offers Petra immunity and a fee to certify Ada's death. He is polite, reasonable, and utterly serious. Beat: temptation dressed as professionalism.

chapters.title: Night at the Parish Tower
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She decides to run — the same night Petra decides to stay. Their paths cross in the archive; the confession letter, the will, and the truth finally sit on the same table. Beat: love against duty, spoken aloud at last.

chapters.title: The Fire in the Filing Room
chapters.summary: Climax, part one. The investigator breaks into the parish office for the records; Ada sets the archive ablaze to destroy the paper trail, and Petra must choose between saving the documents that could clear Edmund's name and the woman they would condemn. Beat: everything burns; only a choice remains.

chapters.title: Ashes and Signatures
chapters.summary: Climax, part two, Petra's POV. Petra confronts the investigator with what survived the fire: nothing, except the confession she now claims never existed. He leaves with no case. Beat: victory that feels like complicity.

chapters.title: The Will Petra Writes
chapters.summary: Petra drafts a new will, dated correctly, leaving the estate to the village — and quietly transfers the tower flat to a tenant named Ada Marsh. Beat: forgery as an act of love.

chapters.title: What the Living Owe the Dead
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. At Edmund's grave, she and Petra speak honestly for the first time. Ada chooses to stay, alive under a small new name, and asks Petra what it costs to carry a secret. Beat: grief, gratitude, and the beginning of something tender.

chapters.title: Postmarked Marlow St. Cuthbert
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Petra's POV, one year later. A letter arrives at her office in Edmund's handwriting — a second confession, hidden in the will's lining, naming Petra as the one who must decide. She reads it, feeds it to the fire, and mails one blank page back to the village. Beat: resolution as inheritance — some truths are kept, not told.
